analysis.one_liner: Requires tax-exempt hospitals to reinvest their tax breaks in patient care and bill assistance patients at Medicare rates.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee since April 2025 with no cosponsors, no committee action, and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make tax-exempt hospitals earn their federal, state, and local tax breaks by spending at least that much each year on free or discounted care, staff training, research, and equipment — and buying up doctors' practices or hospitals wouldn't count, and new buildings could cover no more than half the requirement. It would also cap what financially struggling patients are billed at Medicare rates rather than full sticker prices, bar hospitals from limiting how many Medicare and Medicaid patients they see, and order government watchdogs to audit hospitals' charity-care policies and the IRS's enforcement of the new standard. Hospitals that failed could lose their tax exemption.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who face large hospital bills — especially uninsured or underinsured patients who would be billed at Medicare rates instead of full charges under a hospital's financial assistance policy. Communities near nonprofit hospitals would benefit from a required community board and a guarantee that Medicare and Medicaid patients are not turned away or capped. Taxpayers also gain if hospitals must reinvest the full value of their tax exemptions rather than pocketing them.

how_it_helps.text: Caps charges to financial-assistance-eligible patients at Medicare rates, ending the common practice of billing uninsured and underinsured patients far more than insurers pay.

Requires nonprofit hospitals to spend at least the full value of their federal, state, and local tax exemptions each year on free or discounted care, training, research, and equipment — with acquisitions of physician practices and care organizations excluded and building spending capped at half the requirement.
Requires hospitals to treat Medicare and Medicaid patients without limiting how many they serve at any site they own, and to have boards drawn from the local community.

Orders the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration to review hospital financial assistance policies and report annually, and the Comptroller General to review IRS enforcement of the new standard and report to the tax-writing committees.

analysis.who_pays: Nonprofit hospital organizations. They would face a spending requirement equal to 100% of the value of their tax exemptions, would collect less from assistance-eligible patients whose bills would be capped at Medicare rates, and could lose their federal tax exemption if they fail the new standard. Some of that cost would be offset by the exemption itself remaining valuable only if they comply.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals could satisfy up to half of the spending requirement with facilities and equipment improvements, so money could go to buildings rather than direct patient care; only free or discounted care, training, and research would cover the rest.

The core requirement hinges on measuring the dollar value of a hospital's federal, state, and local tax exemptions each year — a valuation that is inherently complex and could be disputed, making compliance and enforcement difficult.

The 100% threshold is a heavy mandate: hospitals operating on thin margins — particularly rural or safety-net systems — could reduce services, restructure, or give up nonprofit status rather than comply, which could leave some communities with less local care.
Compliance and reporting costs for hospitals and enforcement workload for the IRS, TIGTA, and GAO would grow, with no new funding specified in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are real: billing assistance-eligible patients at Medicare rates and barring hospitals from capping Medicare and Medicaid patients would directly cut a major source of medical debt, and requiring hospitals to reinvest their tax breaks addresses a widely criticized gap in nonprofit hospital accountability. But the design is imperfect — letting buildings count for half the requirement dilutes the benefit, and the tax-exemption valuation standard would be hard to measure and enforce. On balance the bill aims squarely at a genuine public problem, with the main risks being enforcement difficulty and pressure on marginally financed hospitals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it, and Congress is still in session, so it sits with no vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 24, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.
No other House member has signed on as a cosponsor.
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 119th Congress runs through January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has changed yet. Nonprofit hospitals keep their current tax treatment and billing practices, and no one has moved to advance or block the bill; whether patients ever gain depends on whether it ever gets a committee hearing and a vote.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no colleagues signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; has taken no action on it
against.what_they_did: Has held the bill since its April 2025 referral without a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so no partisan split is on the record; the bill has a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill's central target: tax-exempt hospitals would have to spend at least the full value of their tax exemptions on community benefit and cap bills to assistance-eligible patients at Medicare rates, with their tax exemption at stake if they fall short. Today many nonprofit hospitals receive large tax breaks while billing uninsured patients full charges, so the industry's financial interest here runs against patients.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital chains and physician-practice acquirers
industries.note: The bill excludes acquisitions of physician practices, hospitals, and surgery centers from nonprofits' community-benefit spending, which would slow nonprofit buying sprees that for-profit buyers compete in; if nonprofits lost tax exemptions, for-profit operators could gain market share. Neither effect directly benefits patients.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors that has sat untouched in the Ways and Means Committee since April 2025 is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote this Congress; unless it attracts cosponsors and committee leadership schedules it, it will probably die when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
